kapak.alt: Site of lesion and the Metz test

youtube.baslik: Acoustic Reflex Patterns and Site of Lesion | Lesson 109 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
When ipsilateral and contralateral acoustic reflex findings are read together, conductive, cochlear, retrocochlear, brainstem and facial nerve patterns emerge. In this lesson we interpret the four-measurement reflex table, the Metz test and sample patterns step by step.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Jerger S, Jerger J (1977), Diagnostic value of crossed versus uncrossed acoustic reflexes: eighth nerve and brain stem disorders, Archives of Otolaryngology; Metz O (1952), Threshold of reflex contractions of muscles of middle ear and recruitment of loudness, Archives of Otolaryngology; Gelfand SA, Schwander T, Silman S (1990), Acoustic reflex thresholds in normal and cochlear-impaired ears, Journal of Speech and Hearing Disorders; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; BSA, Recommended Procedure: Tympanometry and Acoustic Reflex Thresholds.

sahneler.baslik: Acoustic Reflex *Patterns* and Site of Lesion
sahneler.alt: Estimating the site of lesion with the acoustic reflex
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson, we will learn how the patterns formed by acoustic reflex findings help us estimate where a problem lies.
With sample tables, we will look at conductive, cochlear, retrocochlear, brainstem and facial nerve patterns, and at the Metz test.
To read reflex patterns, let us first be clear about the four measurements made in every patient.
In this lesson, we name each measurement by the ear that receives the stimulus; this is a common convention.
In the right ipsilateral measurement, both the stimulus and the probe are in the right ear.
In the right contralateral measurement, the stimulus goes to the right ear, and the reflex is measured with the probe in the left ear.
The same two measurements are repeated for the left ear, which gives a table of four measurements.
For each finding, we ask two questions: is the problem on the stimulus side, or on the probe side?
The stimulus side reflects the sensory limb of the arc; the probe side reflects that ear's middle ear and facial nerve.

notlar.metin: Probe side: middle ear and CN VII

cumleler: Splitting the reflex arc into two limbs makes the patterns easier to understand.
The sensory, or afferent, limb is made up of the cochlea and the auditory nerve of the stimulated ear.
If there is a problem in this limb, a stimulus to that ear affects both the ipsilateral and the contralateral reflex.
The motor, or efferent, limb is the facial nerve and the stapedius muscle; it is measured with the probe in the ear on that side.
If there is a problem in this limb, or in the middle ear holding the probe, measurements with the probe in that ear are affected.
The pathways that cross in the brainstem are what the two contralateral measurements have in common.
First example: the right ear has a moderate conductive hearing loss, and the left ear is normal.
In the right ipsilateral measurement, the probe is in the right ear and no reflex is recorded.
In the left contralateral measurement, the probe is also on the right; even though the left ear is normal, there is again no reflex.
In the right contralateral measurement, the stimulus goes to the conductive ear; the threshold rises by about the air-bone gap or is lost.
The left ipsilateral measurement is normal, because both the stimulus and the probe are in the healthy ear.
Even a small air-bone gap in the probe ear often prevents the reflex from being measured.
With a bilateral conductive hearing loss, the reflex is often absent in all four measurements.

notlar.metin: Mild to moderate loss: normal threshold

cumleler: Second example: a sensorineural hearing loss of cochlear origin.
In mild and moderate cochlear losses, reflex thresholds often stay within normal limits, around eighty five dB HL.
So the reflex appears at a lower sensation level than in a normal ear.
Once the loss exceeds about fifty to sixty dB HL, the reflex threshold starts to rise.
With more severe losses, the reflex is often absent up to the safe test limit.
This graph is schematic; in the clinic, norms from large samples, such as the ninetieth percentiles of Gelfand and colleagues, are used.
In a cochlear loss, both measurements with the stimulus in the affected ear are affected in the same way; the probe side causes no problem.

cumleler.yazi: The classic method that uses the gap between the reflex threshold and the hearing threshold is called the Metz recruitment test.
The test is named after the Danish researcher Otto Metz.

cumleler: In a normal hearing ear, the reflex appears about seventy to one hundred decibels above the hearing threshold.
If the gap is sixty decibels or less, the finding suggests that loudness grows quickly above threshold, which is recruitment.
In this example, at one thousand hertz the hearing threshold is sixty and the reflex threshold one hundred dB HL; the gap is only forty.
This finding is consistent with a hearing loss of cochlear origin.

cumleler.yazi: However, the Metz test does not separate the two on its own; a similar finding can occur with a retrocochlear lesion.

cumleler: This is why, today, the finding is evaluated together with the other patterns and the test battery.
Third example: a lesion affecting the right auditory nerve, that is, a retrocochlear lesion.
Here, in both measurements with the stimulus in the right ear, the reflex is absent or clearly elevated.
The key clue is that the reflex finding is out of proportion to the degree of hearing loss.
Measurements with the stimulus in the left ear are normal, because the right facial nerve and the right middle ear are intact.
For example, a completely absent reflex in an ear whose threshold is only thirty dB HL is striking.
A finding like this brings to mind auditory nerve lesions such as vestibular schwannoma and calls for further assessment.
Reflex decay can also be checked in the same ear; we will see this in the next lesson.
Let us look at a sample audiogram that fits this pattern: mild hearing loss in the right ear and normal hearing in the left.
Both tympanograms are type A, so both middle ears appear normal.
With the stimulus in the right ear, no reflex is recorded up to the highest safe level tested.
In a mild loss, the reflex threshold is expected to be within normal limits, so the finding is out of proportion.
This picture calls for referral for further assessment; the example is for teaching.
The fourth example is a lesion in the middle of the brainstem that affects the crossing pathways.
Here, in both contralateral measurements, the reflex is absent or clearly elevated.
The ipsilateral measurements can stay normal, because the same-side pathway is completed without crossing.
Hearing thresholds may be normal or near normal, which makes the finding even more meaningful.
This pattern can be seen in conditions that affect the brainstem, such as multiple sclerosis, or with masses.
Here we clearly see why ipsilateral and contralateral measurements should be done together.
Fifth example: the right facial nerve is affected before the point where its stapedius branch leaves.
In both measurements with the probe in the right ear, the reflex is absent, because the right stapedius cannot contract.
Measurements with the probe in the left ear are normal.
This pattern looks like a conductive loss in the probe ear; the tympanogram and the audiogram tell them apart.
With a facial nerve problem, hearing and the tympanogram are usually normal.

cumleler.yazi: In Bell's palsy, a present reflex may suggest that the lesion lies distal to the origin of the stapedius branch.

cumleler: The return of the reflex over time can also be followed as a sign of recovery.
With a conductive loss or a facial nerve problem, measurements with the probe in the affected ear are disturbed.
With a severe cochlear loss, the reflex rises or disappears when the stimulus goes to the affected ear.
With an auditory nerve lesion, the stimulus side is also affected, but the finding is out of proportion to the degree of hearing loss.
With a lesion in the middle of the brainstem, both contralateral measurements are disturbed and the ipsilaterals are spared.
For a facial nerve problem, a normal tympanogram and a normal audiogram are what tell it apart.
Instead of memorizing this table, thinking about the two limbs of the arc leads to the right answer in every new case.
When interpreting a reflex table, first look at the tympanograms of both ears.
Then note the degree of loss in each ear from the audiogram, because the expected reflex threshold depends on it.
Next, mark which of the four measurements are absent or elevated.
Look for what the abnormal measurements share: the same stimulus ear, the same probe ear, or both contralaterals?
If the finding cannot be explained by the degree of loss, state this clearly in the report.
As a last step, combine the result with tests such as speech tests and the auditory brainstem response, and with the physician's assessment.

sahneler.metin: Before interpreting an absent reflex, check the tympanogram of the probe ear. A small conductive problem in the ear holding the probe can change the whole pattern.
cumleler: A practical tip: when you see a pattern in a reflex table, question the probe ear first.
Clear negative pressure or effusion in the probe ear can abolish reflexes on its own and create a false pattern.
If in doubt, repeat the measurement with the pressure set to the peak pressure, and check the probe fit.
A true nerve or brainstem pattern is still seen consistently after these checks.

ogeler.metin: Does not rule out a lesion

cumleler: Reflex patterns are a powerful tool, but they have some limitations.
Normal reflexes do not rule out a retrocochlear lesion; reflexes can be normal, especially with small tumors.
In an ear with severe hearing loss, an absent reflex makes it hard to separate a neural problem from a cochlear loss.
In a small share of people with normal hearing, the reflex may be absent, especially at high frequencies.
This is why reflex findings do not make a diagnosis on their own; they strengthen or weaken a possibility.
The decision about whether imaging is needed always belongs to the physician.

maddeler.metin: _Probe_ side: middle ear and CN VII

cumleler: Abnormal results tied to the stimulus ear suggest the sensory limb of the arc, that is, the cochlea and the auditory nerve.
Abnormal results tied to the probe ear suggest a conductive problem in that ear, or the facial nerve.
When both contralateral measurements are abnormal together, a problem in the middle of the brainstem comes to mind.

cumleler.yazi: In the Metz test, a gap of sixty decibels or less between the reflex and hearing thresholds suggests recruitment.

sahneler.soru: Right ear 30 dB HL, normal tympanogram, no reflex with right stimulus. What is suspected?
sahneler.aciklama: An absent reflex _out of proportion_ to a mild loss raises questions about the auditory nerve on the stimulus side.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: The right ear is at thirty dB HL, the tympanogram is normal, and right stimulation gives no reflex. What is suspected?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: a possible right retrocochlear lesion.
An absent reflex out of proportion to a mild loss questions the auditory nerve on the stimulus side and calls for further assessment.
In the next lesson, we will look at the reflex decay test, which measures whether the reflex fades during a sustained sound.
